title: Part 1, Chapter 6
paragraphs: Raskolnikov later found out why the peddler and his wife had invited Lizaveta. It was a perfectly ordinary matter, nothing unusual about it. A family that had recently moved to the city, fallen on hard times, was selling off their household goods and clothes -- mostly women's things. Since the items would fetch little at market, they were looking for a dealer. This was Lizaveta's line of work. She handled these kinds of transactions regularly and had a reputation for honesty, always naming a fair price and sticking to it. She rarely said much and, as already mentioned, was extremely meek and timid.

But Raskolnikov had grown superstitious lately. The traces of superstition lingered in him long afterward and were nearly impossible to shake. In everything that happened, he was always inclined to see something strange and mysterious, as if there were some peculiar force at work, some pattern of meaningful coincidences. The previous winter, a student he knew named Pokorev, who was leaving for Kharkov, had happened to mention in conversation the address of Alyona Ivanovna, the old pawnbroker, in case Raskolnikov ever needed to pawn something. For a long time he didn't go. He had tutoring work and was getting by. Six weeks ago he had remembered the address. He had two things he could pawn: his father's old silver watch and a little gold ring with three red stones, a farewell gift from his sister. He decided to take the ring. From the moment he first laid eyes on the old woman, he felt an overwhelming revulsion for her, though he knew nothing particular about her. He got two rubles from her and stopped at a miserable little tavern on his way home. He ordered tea, sat down, and sank into deep thought. A strange idea was pecking at his brain like a chick in an egg, and it absorbed him completely.

At the next table, almost beside him, sat a student he didn't know and had never seen, along with a young officer. They had just played billiards and were drinking tea. Suddenly he heard the student mention the pawnbroker Alyona Ivanovna to the officer and give him her address. This alone seemed strange to Raskolnikov -- he had just come from her, and here was someone mentioning her name. Of course it was coincidence, but he couldn't shake the extraordinary impression, as if someone were speaking specifically for his benefit. The student began telling his friend various details about Alyona Ivanovna.

"She's first-rate," he said. "You can always get money from her. She's rich as a Rothschild -- could give you five thousand rubles at a time, and she doesn't turn down pledges for a single ruble. Lots of our guys have dealt with her. But she's a terrible old witch...."

He went on describing how spiteful and unpredictable she was -- how if your interest payment was even one day late, the pledge was gone; how she gave a quarter of an item's value and charged five, even seven percent a month, and so on. The student chattered away, mentioning that she had a sister, Lizaveta, whom the nasty creature constantly beat and kept in total submission, like a small child, even though Lizaveta was nearly six feet tall.
"Now there's a phenomenon for you," the student said with a laugh.

They started discussing Lizaveta. The student spoke about her with a strange kind of relish, laughing constantly, while the officer listened with interest and asked him to send Lizaveta over to do some mending. Raskolnikov didn't miss a word and learned everything. Lizaveta was younger than the old woman and was her half-sister from a different mother. She was thirty-five. She worked day and night for her sister -- cooking, cleaning, sewing, taking charwoman jobs -- and handed over everything she earned. She didn't dare accept any work without her sister's permission. The old woman had already made her will, and Lizaveta knew about it: she would inherit nothing but some furniture -- chairs and the like. All the money was left to a monastery in N----- province, for prayers to be said for the old woman's soul in perpetuity. Lizaveta was of a lower social rank than her sister, unmarried, and remarkably ungainly in appearance -- very tall, with long feet that seemed to turn outward. She always wore battered goatskin shoes but was clean in her person. What the student found most surprising and amusing was the fact that Lizaveta was constantly pregnant.
"But you said she's ugly?" the officer remarked.

"Yes, she's dark-skinned and looks like a soldier in a dress, but actually she's not ugly at all. She has such a kind face, and kind eyes. Strikingly so. The proof is that plenty of men find her attractive. She's such a soft, gentle creature -- puts up with anything, always willing, ready for anything. And her smile is genuinely sweet."
"Sounds like you find her attractive yourself," the officer laughed.

"It's her oddness. But here's what I wanted to say. I could kill that damn old woman and take her money -- I'm telling you -- without the slightest pang of conscience," the student added with passion. The officer laughed again. Raskolnikov shuddered. How strange this was!

"Listen, I want to ask you a serious question," the student went on, heated. "I was joking, of course, but think about it. On one side you have a stupid, senseless, worthless, spiteful, sick, horrible old woman, not merely useless but actively harmful -- who has no idea why she's even alive, and who'll die in a day or two anyway. You follow? You follow?"
"Yes, yes, I follow," the officer answered, watching his excited friend closely.

"Now listen. On the other side, you have young lives being thrown away by the thousands for lack of help, everywhere you look! A hundred thousand good deeds could be done with that old woman's money -- money that's going to be buried in a monastery! Hundreds, maybe thousands of people could be set on the right path. Dozens of families saved from poverty, ruin, depravity, disease -- all with her money. Kill her, take the money, and devote yourself to serving humanity and the common good. What do you think -- wouldn't one tiny crime be erased by thousands of good deeds? One life for a hundred lives in return -- it's simple math! Besides, what is the life of that sickly, stupid, spiteful old woman worth in the grand scale of things? No more than the life of a louse or a cockroach -- less, actually, because the old woman is doing harm. She's destroying other people's lives. The other day she bit Lizaveta's finger out of sheer spite -- it nearly had to be amputated."
"Of course she doesn't deserve to live," the officer agreed. "But that's just how things are -- it's nature."

"Sure, brother, but we have to correct and redirect nature. Without that, we'd drown in an ocean of prejudice. Without that, there would never have been a single great man. People talk about duty, conscience -- I don't want to say anything against duty and conscience -- but what exactly do we mean by them? Wait, let me ask you another question. Listen!"
"No, wait -- I'll ask you a question. Listen!"
"Go ahead."
"You're making speeches and theorizing, but tell me: would you kill the old woman _yourself_?"
"Of course not! I was just arguing the principle of the thing.... It has nothing to do with me personally...."
"Well, I think if you wouldn't do it yourself, then there's no justice in it at all.... Let's play another game."

Raskolnikov was deeply shaken. Of course, it was all just typical student talk -- the kind of thing he had heard many times before, in different forms and on different topics. But why had he happened to overhear this particular conversation, with these particular ideas, at the precise moment when his own brain was conceiving... _the very same ideas_? And why, at the very moment he had carried away the germ of his idea from the old woman's apartment, had he stumbled upon a conversation about her? This coincidence always struck him as strange. This trivial tavern talk would have an enormous influence on everything that followed -- as though something had been lying in wait, something preordained, some guiding hint....

After returning from the Hay Market, he threw himself on the sofa and sat motionless for a full hour. Meanwhile it grew dark. He had no candle, and it didn't even occur to him to light one. He could never afterward remember whether he had been thinking about anything during that time. At last he felt the familiar fever and chills returning, and realized with relief that he could lie down on the sofa. Soon a heavy, leaden sleep descended on him, crushing him down.

He slept an extraordinarily long time, without dreaming. Nastasya came into his room at ten the next morning and had trouble waking him. She brought tea and bread. The tea was once again the second brewing, served in her own teapot.
"Good grief, how he sleeps!" she cried indignantly. "Always sleeping!"
He got up with effort. His head ached. He stood, paced his tiny room, and collapsed back onto the sofa.
"Going back to sleep?" Nastasya exclaimed. "Are you sick?"
He didn't answer.
"Want some tea?"
"Later," he said with effort, closing his eyes and turning to the wall.
Nastasya stood over him.

"Maybe he really is sick," she said, turned, and left. She came back at two with soup. He was lying in the same position. The tea was untouched. Nastasya felt genuinely offended and began shaking him awake angrily.
"Why are you lying there like a log?" she shouted, looking at him with disgust.
He sat up but said nothing, staring at the floor.
"Are you sick or not?" Nastasya demanded, getting no answer again. "You should go outside and get some air. Are you going to eat this or not?"
"Later," he said weakly. "Go away."
He waved her out.
She lingered a moment, looked at him with pity, and left.
A few minutes later he raised his eyes and stared for a long time at the tea and the soup. Then he picked up the bread, took the spoon, and began to eat.

He ate a little -- three or four spoonfuls, without appetite, mechanically. His headache was better. After eating he lay back on the sofa, but couldn't sleep. He lay still, face down in the pillow, haunted by daydreams -- strange daydreams. In one that kept recurring, he imagined he was in Africa, in Egypt, at some oasis. The caravan was resting. The camels lay peacefully. Palm trees formed a perfect circle around them. Everyone was eating. But he was drinking water from a spring that flowed gurgling nearby. And it was so cool -- wonderful, wonderful -- blue, cold water running over colored stones and over clean sand that glittered like gold.... Suddenly he heard a clock strike. He flinched, roused himself, raised his head, looked out the window, saw how late it was, and sprang up wide awake as though someone had yanked him off the sofa. He crept to the door on tiptoe, opened it silently, and began listening on the staircase. His heart was pounding. But the stairs were quiet -- everyone seemed to be asleep.... It struck him as strange, monstrous, that he could have slept in such oblivion since the day before and had done nothing, prepared nothing.... And it might already have struck six. His drowsiness and confusion gave way to an extraordinary, feverish, almost frantic haste. But there was little to prepare. He focused all his energy on thinking of everything and forgetting nothing, while his heart pounded so hard he could barely breathe. First he had to make a loop and sew it into his overcoat -- a moment's work. He rummaged under his pillow and pulled from the linen stuffed under it an old, worn-out, unwashed shirt. From its rags he tore a long strip, about two inches wide and sixteen inches long. He folded the strip in two, took off his broad, sturdy summer overcoat -- thick cotton, his only outer garment -- and began sewing both ends of the strip to the inside, under the left armhole. His hands trembled as he sewed, but he managed it, and when he put the coat back on, nothing showed from the outside. The needle and thread had been ready for a long time and lay on his table wrapped in paper. As for the loop, it was his own clever design: the loop was meant for the axe. It was impossible to carry an axe through the street in his hands. Hidden under his coat, he would still have to hold it, which would be noticeable. Now he only had to slip the axe head through the loop, and it would hang silently under his arm on the inside. By putting his hand in his coat pocket, he could hold the end of the handle the whole way, keeping it from swinging. And since the coat was very full -- practically a sack -- nobody would be able to tell from the outside that his hand was holding something in the pocket. He had designed this loop two weeks earlier.

When he was finished, he thrust his hand into a small gap between the sofa and the floor, felt around in the left corner, and pulled out the _pledge_ -- prepared long ago and hidden there. This pledge was nothing but a smoothly planed piece of wood, about the size and thickness of a silver cigarette case. He had found it during one of his wanderings, in a courtyard where some kind of workshop was set up. Later he had added a thin, smooth piece of iron that he'd also picked up in the street. Placing the iron -- slightly smaller -- on the piece of wood, he had bound them tightly together, wrapping thread around and around them, then wrapped the whole thing neatly in clean white paper and tied the package so it would be very difficult to undo. This was to distract the old woman for a moment while she struggled with the knot, buying him time. The iron strip was added for weight, so she wouldn't immediately guess the "object" was made of wood. All of this had been stored under his sofa. He had just pulled out the pledge when he heard someone shout in the yard:
"It struck six ages ago."
"Ages ago! My God!"

He rushed to the door, listened, grabbed his hat, and began descending his thirteen steps cautiously, noiselessly, like a cat. The most important thing still remained: stealing the axe from the kitchen. He had decided long ago that the deed must be done with an axe. He also had a folding pocketknife, but he couldn't rely on the knife, and even less on his own strength, so he had settled on the axe. We might note in passing a peculiarity about all his final decisions in this matter: the more definite they became, the more grotesque and absurd they instantly appeared to him. Despite all his agonizing inner struggle, he could never for a single moment truly believe he would carry out his plan.

And indeed, if everything had ever been considered down to the last detail and definitively settled, with no uncertainty remaining, he would probably have abandoned the whole thing as something absurd, monstrous, and impossible. But a whole mass of unsettled points and uncertainties remained. As for getting the axe, this trivial matter caused him no worry, because nothing could be easier. Nastasya was constantly out of the house, especially in the evenings -- running to neighbors or to a shop -- and always left the door open. It was the one thing the landlady was always scolding her about. So when the time came, he would simply have to slip into the kitchen, take the axe, and an hour later -- when everything was over -- go back and replace it. But there were doubts. Suppose he came back an hour later to return it and Nastasya was back and in the kitchen. He would have to walk past and wait for her to leave again. But what if in the meantime she missed the axe, looked for it, raised an alarm -- that would mean suspicion, or at least grounds for it.

But these were all trivial details he hadn't even begun to consider, and had no time for. He was focused on the main thing, putting off minor details until _he could believe in the whole enterprise_. But that seemed utterly impossible. At least it seemed so to him. He couldn't imagine, for instance, that he would someday stop thinking, get up, and simply go there.... Even his recent experiment -- his visit to the old woman's to survey the place -- had been merely an attempt at an experiment, far from the real thing, as if he were saying, "Come on, let's try it out -- why just dream about it!" -- and he had immediately broken down and fled in a fury of self-contempt. Meanwhile, on the moral question, his analysis seemed complete. His reasoning had been honed razor-sharp, and he could find no rational objections within himself. But in the end, he simply stopped believing in himself and stubbornly, slavishly kept groping for arguments in all directions, as though some force were pushing and pulling him toward it.

Long before -- much earlier -- he had been preoccupied with one question: why are almost all crimes so poorly concealed and so easily detected, and why do almost all criminals leave such obvious traces? He had gradually reached many different and curious conclusions. In his view, the main reason lay not so much in the material difficulty of concealing a crime as in the criminal himself. Nearly every criminal experiences a collapse of willpower and reasoning ability -- a childish, phenomenal recklessness -- at the very moment when caution and prudence are most essential. He was convinced that this eclipse of reason and failure of will attacks a person like a disease, develops gradually, reaches its peak just before the crime is committed, continues with equal intensity during the crime itself and for some time afterward -- varying by individual -- and then passes, like any other illness. The question of whether the disease causes the crime, or whether the crime by its very nature always brings something like disease with it, he did not yet feel able to answer.

Having reached these conclusions, he decided that in his own case there would be no such morbid reaction, that his reason and will would remain intact during the execution of his plan, for the simple reason that his plan was "not a crime".... We will skip the process by which he arrived at this last conclusion -- we have gotten too far ahead already.... We will only add that the practical, purely material difficulties occupied a secondary place in his mind. "You just need to keep your willpower and reasoning faculties intact, and you'll deal with all of it when the time comes, once you've thoroughly familiarized yourself with every detail...." But this preparation had never actually begun. His final decisions were what he trusted least, and when the hour struck, everything happened quite differently -- almost accidentally, almost by surprise.

One minor circumstance wrecked his plan before he had even reached the bottom of the staircase. When he reached the landlady's kitchen, its door open as usual, he glanced in cautiously to check whether Nastasya was out and whether the landlady's own door was closed, so she wouldn't peek out when he went in for the axe. But to his astonishment, Nastasya was not only home -- she was right there in the kitchen, pulling laundry from a basket and hanging it on a line. Seeing him, she stopped, turned, and stared at him the whole time he was passing. He looked away and walked past as though he hadn't noticed anything. But it was all over. He didn't have the axe! He was devastated.
"What made me think," he muttered as he passed through the gateway, "what made me think she would definitely be out at that exact moment? Why, why, why was I so sure of it?"
He felt crushed, humiliated. He could have laughed at himself in his rage.... A dull, animal fury boiled inside him.

He stood in the gateway, hesitating. Going out for a walk to keep up appearances was revolting. Going back to his room was even worse. "And what a chance I've lost -- forever!" he muttered, standing aimlessly in the gateway, directly across from the porter's small, dark room, which was also open. Suddenly he froze. From the porter's room, barely two steps away, something shiny under the bench on the right caught his eye.... He looked around -- nobody. He approached the room on tiptoe, went down two steps, and called out weakly for the porter. "Right -- not home. Somewhere nearby though, in the yard, since the door is wide open." He lunged for the axe (it was an axe) and pulled it from under the bench, where it lay between two blocks of wood. Immediately, before stepping out, he fastened it in the loop, shoved both hands in his pockets, and walked out of the room. No one had noticed him. "When reason fails, the devil helps!" he thought with a strange grin. This stroke of luck raised his spirits enormously.

He walked along quietly and steadily, without hurrying, to avoid raising suspicion. He barely looked at the people he passed, trying not to meet anyone's eyes, making himself as inconspicuous as possible. Suddenly he thought of his hat. "For God's sake! I had money the day before yesterday and didn't buy a cap to wear instead!" A curse rose from the depths of his soul.

Glancing into a shop out of the corner of his eye, he saw by a wall clock that it was ten minutes past seven. He had to hurry and at the same time take a roundabout route to approach the building from the other side....

Whenever he had imagined all this beforehand, he had sometimes thought he would be very afraid. But he wasn't very afraid now -- not afraid at all, in fact. His mind was occupied with irrelevant things, though nothing for long. Passing the Yusupov Garden, he found himself absorbed in the idea of building great fountains and how they would cool the air in all the city squares. Gradually he became convinced that if the Summer Garden were extended to the Field of Mars and perhaps connected to the Mikhailovsky Palace garden, it would be a splendid thing, a great benefit to the city. Then he got interested in the question of why, in all great cities, people are not simply forced by necessity but seem somehow peculiarly drawn to live in exactly those parts of town where there are no gardens, no fountains -- where there is the most filth and stench and every kind of squalor. Then his own walks through the Hay Market came to mind, and for a moment he snapped back to reality. "What nonsense!" he thought. "Better not to think about anything at all!"

"People being led to execution probably clutch mentally at every object they pass along the way," flashed through his mind, but only flashed -- like lightning. He pushed the thought away.... And now he was close. Here was the building. Here was the gate. Suddenly a clock struck once somewhere. "What! Can it already be half past seven? Impossible -- it must be fast!"

Luckily, everything went smoothly at the gate again. At that very moment, as if arranged for his benefit, a huge hay cart had just driven in through the gateway, completely screening him as he passed under it. The wagon had barely cleared the entrance into the yard before he had slipped to the right in a flash. On the other side of the wagon he could hear shouting and arguing, but no one noticed him and no one crossed his path. Many windows facing that huge rectangular courtyard were open, but he didn't raise his head -- he didn't have the strength. The staircase leading to the old woman's apartment was right there, just to the right of the gateway. He was already on the stairs....

He drew a breath, pressed his hand to his hammering heart, felt for the axe one more time and adjusted it, then began climbing the stairs softly and cautiously, listening at every step. But the staircase was completely deserted. All the doors were shut. He met no one. One apartment on the first floor was wide open and painters were working inside, but they didn't glance at him. He paused, thought for a moment, and continued. "It would be better if they weren't here, of course, but... they're two floors below."

And there was the fourth floor. There was the door. There was the apartment across the hall -- the empty one. The apartment below the old woman's seemed vacant too: the business card nailed to the door had been torn off -- the tenants had moved away!... He was out of breath. For one instant the thought floated through his mind: "Should I go back?" But he gave himself no answer and began listening at the old woman's door. Dead silence. Then he listened on the staircase -- listened long and hard... then took one last look around, pulled himself together, straightened up, and tested the axe in the loop one more time. "Am I very pale?" he wondered. "Is it obvious I'm agitated? She's suspicious.... Maybe I should wait a bit longer... until my heart stops pounding?"

But his heart wouldn't stop. On the contrary, as if to spite him, it pounded harder and harder. He couldn't stand it any longer. He slowly reached out and rang the bell. Half a minute later, he rang again, louder.

No answer. Ringing further was pointless and would attract attention. The old woman was certainly home, but she was suspicious and alone. He had some knowledge of her habits... and once more he pressed his ear to the door. Either his senses were extraordinarily heightened -- which seems hard to believe -- or the sound was truly very distinct. He suddenly heard something like a hand carefully touching the lock, and the rustle of fabric right at the door. Someone was standing silently pressed against the lock on the other side, secretly listening from within, just as he was doing from without, apparently with her ear to the door.... He shifted slightly on purpose and muttered something aloud so he wouldn't seem to be hiding, then rang a third time -- quietly, calmly, without impatience. Looking back on it later, that moment stood out in his memory with terrifying clarity, forever. He could not understand how he had possessed such cunning, because his mind seemed clouded at moments and he was barely aware of his own body.... An instant later, he heard the latch being unfastened.
